raw_response.headline_result_summary: Across 115 U.S. municipally-owned water utilities in the 1965 AWWA survey, state public utility commission (PUC) regulation of municipal water rate structures (n = 27 utilities in 5 states) is associated with significantly lower residential deadweight monopoly welfare loss (as a percentage of the residential customer's annual water bill/revenue) than local regulation by city councils or water commissions (n = 88 utilities): 5.2% vs. 9.6% in unweighted Model 1 (printed difference = -4.6 percentage points, t = -4.58, p < 0.01 one-tailed; 46% lower relatively) and 6.15% vs. 10.39% in bill-weighted Model 2 (difference = -4.24 percentage points, t = -2.71, p < 0.01 one-tailed; 41% lower relatively). Substantively, the outcome—Harberger allocative deadweight welfare loss from price exceeding long-run marginal cost among already-connected municipal customers—is an indirect economic-efficiency/pricing-markup metric (indirect_or_non_access_outcome) rather than a direct measure of household water connection, coverage, reliability, or income-share affordability; however, if mapped onto residential tariff/consumer-pricing protection, the negative raw sign corresponds to a favorable effect of state PUC regulation in restraining monopoly pricing exaction against residential water consumers.
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Indirect/non-access outcome vs. household access conflation: Table 2 measures the Harberger deadweight allocative welfare loss triangle (W = (1/2)Qe(P - LRMC)^2/P divided by residential annual revenue P*Q) among already-served municipal residential customers. It does not measure household water connection, coverage, disconnection, continuity, water quality, or household income affordability, nor does the paper separately report group means for residential water price (P) or annual water bills (P*Q); the author explicitly notes 'the low cost of water' ($40-$80 illustrative annual bills), peak demand driven by 'residential lawn sprinkling demand', and unmodeled subsidy costs required if P = LRMC under economies of scale. 2. Inverse polarity / sign-flip trap: Because higher values of monopoly welfare loss (%) mean worse supra-marginal-cost pricing exaction against residential customers, the negative raw difference (-4.6 pp, t = -4.58; -4.24 pp, t = -2.71) means state PUC regulation reduces residential welfare loss (favorable to residential consumers if treated as an affordability/pricing-protection proxy); equating the negative raw sign with an adverse effect flips the conclusion. 3. Exposure pole orientation (state PUC regulation vs. local municipal regulation): Table 2 defines Difference as State-regulated minus Locally-regulated (referred to in Note 23 as 'regulated' vs. 'unregulated' groups). Treating local municipal control/decentralization as the focal exposure flips the raw sign to positive (+4.6 and +4.24 pp, indicating greater monopoly welfare loss under local regulation). 4. Arithmetic discrepancy and percentage-point vs. relative-percent reporting: In Model 1, the printed group means are 5.2% and 9.6% (exact difference = -4.4 pp), whereas Table 2 and p. 237 print -4.6 pp (consistent with t = -4.58 given SEs .818 and .583); additionally, p. 237 reports absolute percentage-point differences (-4.6% and -4.24%), while p. 238 reports relative reductions (46% and 41% lower). 5. Intermediate regressions do not test regulation: Equations [1] (total variable cost, n = 95), [3] (distribution loss, n = 95, where residential volume Qr has coefficient .036, t = 1.17, non-significant), and [6] (total fixed cost, n = 87; note misprint .0157 in Eq. [7] for .01057 from Eq. [6]) are auxiliary cost-imputation steps containing no regulatory variable.
raw_response.study_design: Observational cross-sectional econometric cost-imputation and two-group mean-comparison study of municipally-owned water utilities using 1965 and 1960 American Water Works Association (AWWA) Survey of Operating Data (OLS regressions to estimate utility-specific long-run marginal cost combined with regional demand elasticities, followed by unadjusted unweighted and bill-weighted two-sample t-tests across regulatory regimes)
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Municipally-owned water utilities (residential customer class aggregates). Primary regulatory comparison (Table 2): N = 115 utilities (n = 88 locally-regulated utilities; n = 27 state-regulated utilities in Maine, Indiana, Montana, West Virginia, and Wisconsin). Intermediate OLS cost/loss estimation samples (Section III): n = 95 utilities for total variable cost (Eq. 1) and distribution system water loss (Eq. 3); n = 87 utilities for total fixed cost (Eq. 6).
